tips.title: Break costs, form pays
tips.body: **Higher tier.** **Breaking** bonds needs energy in, so it is **endothermic**. **Forming** bonds gives energy out, so it is **exothermic**. Every bond energy question is just deciding which side is bigger.

tips.title: Negative means exothermic
tips.body: **Higher tier.** The calculation is **broken − formed**, and it describes the **chemicals**. If more came out than went in, the chemicals have **lost** energy, so the answer is **negative** and the reaction is **exothermic**. Positive means endothermic.

tips.title: The hump is not the energy change
tips.body: To decide exothermic or endothermic, look **only** at where the **products** sit compared with the reactants. The height of the hump tells you how hard the reaction is to **start**, and nothing else. Burning petrol has a tall hump and is strongly exothermic.

tips.title: Count every bond in every molecule
tips.body: **Higher tier.** Two water molecules contain **four** O–H bonds, not two. Write out each molecule and count its bonds before multiplying. Counting the molecules instead of the bonds is the single commonest lost mark here.

steps.title: Why reactions need a push to start
steps.body:
A reaction can only happen when particles **collide**, and colliding is not enough on its own. They have to collide **with enough energy**.

The minimum amount of energy that particles must have to react is called the **activation energy**. Below it, particles bounce apart unchanged however often they meet.

That is why a mixture of petrol and air sits quite happily in a fuel tank. The reaction releases a great deal of energy once started, but nothing happens until something supplies the activation energy: a spark.

So two separate quantities describe any reaction, and questions often ask for both.

- The **activation energy**: the push needed to get it going.
- The **overall energy change**: the difference between the energy of the products and the energy of the reactants.

One says how hard it is to start. The other says what you get out. They are independent: a reaction can release a lot of energy and still need a large push.

steps.title: Drawing a reaction profile
steps.body:
A **reaction profile** is an energy level diagram that shows three things at once: the energy of the **reactants**, the energy of the **products**, and the **activation energy** between them.

To draw one that earns full marks:

1. Energy goes up the **vertical** axis; progress of the reaction goes along the **horizontal** axis.
2. Draw a level line for the **reactants** on the left, labelled.
3. Draw a level line for the **products** on the right, labelled. **Below** the reactants for exothermic, **above** for endothermic.
4. Join them with a **curved line that rises to a peak and comes down** again. The curve is the reaction happening.
5. Mark the **activation energy** with an arrow from the **reactant level up to the peak**.
6. Mark the **overall energy change** with an arrow between the **reactant level and the product level**.

The two arrows start in different places, and that is the detail most often lost. The activation energy is measured from the reactants to the **top of the hump**, never from the bottom of the axis and never from the products.

steps.title: Reading a profile the other way
steps.body:
Given a profile, you should be able to say immediately whether the reaction is exothermic or endothermic. Look only at where the **products** sit compared with the **reactants**.

- Products **lower** than reactants: energy has left the chemicals, so the reaction is **exothermic**.
- Products **higher** than reactants: energy has gone into the chemicals, so the reaction is **endothermic**.

The size of the hump tells you nothing about which it is. A tall hump on an exothermic reaction just means it is hard to start, not that it takes energy in overall.

That is worth saying twice, because it is the single commonest mistake on this topic: **the hump is not the energy change**. Petrol burning has a large hump and is strongly exothermic.

steps.title: Higher tier: bonds break, bonds form
steps.body:
This section is **Higher tier only**.

Every reaction does two things, in this order:

- **Energy must be supplied to break bonds** in the reactants. Breaking bonds is always **endothermic**.
- **Energy is released when bonds form** in the products. Making bonds is always **exothermic**.

Which of those two wins decides the whole reaction.

- If **more energy is released forming bonds** than was needed to break them, the reaction is **exothermic**.
- If **more energy is needed to break bonds** than is released forming them, the reaction is **endothermic**.

That gives the calculation:

$$\text{overall change} = \text{energy to break bonds} - \text{energy released forming bonds}$$

A **negative** answer means energy was given out overall, so the reaction is **exothermic**. A **positive** answer means endothermic. The sign is doing real work here, and dropping it loses the final mark.

Bond energies are always **supplied** in the question. You are never expected to recall them.

steps.title: Higher tier: doing the calculation
steps.body:
The method is the same every time. Set it out in the same order and the marks follow even if the arithmetic slips.

1. List every bond **broken**, with its energy, and add them up.
2. List every bond **formed**, with its energy, and add them up.
3. Subtract: **broken minus formed**.
4. Read the sign, and say what it means.

The usual lost mark is forgetting that a molecule can contain several identical bonds, so a water molecule brings **two** O–H bonds to the total, and two water molecules bring four.

steps.title: Going deeper: why the sign comes out the way it does
steps.body:
Students who lose marks here almost always lose them to the **sign**, so it is worth understanding rather than memorising.

The calculation is **energy in minus energy out**. If more comes out than goes in, the subtraction gives a **negative** number. Negative therefore means **energy released**, which is **exothermic**. It looks backwards until you notice that the number describes the **chemicals**, not the surroundings: the chemicals have **lost** energy, so their change is negative.

That also reconciles this topic with the last one. An exothermic reaction leaves the **products with less energy than the reactants** — which is exactly what a negative change says, and exactly what the profile draws as a step downwards. Three descriptions of one fact:

- in words, energy is transferred to the surroundings;
- as a picture, the products sit below the reactants;
- as a number, the overall change is negative.

One further point worth having ready. Bond energies are **mean** values, averaged over many different compounds, so a calculated change is an **estimate** rather than an exact figure. A question asking why a calculated value differs from a measured one is usually asking for that.

And the activation energy is untouched by all of this. It is about how hard the reaction is to **start**, and a catalyst lowers it without changing the overall energy change at all: the reactants and products stay exactly where they were, and only the hump gets shorter.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- Particles react only when they **collide with enough energy**. The minimum needed is the **activation energy**.
- A **reaction profile** shows the reactants, the products, the activation energy and the overall energy change.
- The **activation energy arrow** runs from the **reactants up to the peak**. The **overall change arrow** runs between the **reactants and products levels**. Different starting points.
- Products **below** reactants means **exothermic**; products **above** means **endothermic**.
- The **height of the hump says nothing** about which it is.
- **Higher tier**: **breaking** bonds is **endothermic** (energy supplied); **forming** bonds is **exothermic** (energy released).
- **Higher tier**: **overall change = energy to break bonds − energy released forming bonds.**
- **Higher tier**: a **negative** answer means **exothermic**; a **positive** answer means **endothermic**.
- **Higher tier**: count **every** bond, since two water molecules contain **four** O–H bonds.
- **Higher tier**: bond energies are always **given**, and are **mean** values, so a calculated change is an **estimate**.
- A **catalyst** lowers the activation energy only. The overall energy change is unchanged.

questions.solution: The bonds broken are two hydrogen to hydrogen bonds and one oxygen to oxygen double bond. That is two times four hundred and thirty six, which is eight hundred and seventy two, plus four hundred and ninety eight, giving one thousand three hundred and seventy kilojoules per mole. The bonds formed are the oxygen to hydrogen bonds in two water molecules. Each water molecule has two of them, so four are formed in total, and four times four hundred and sixty four is one thousand eight hundred and fifty six kilojoules per mole. The overall energy change is the energy needed to break bonds minus the energy released when bonds form, which is one thousand three hundred and seventy minus one thousand eight hundred and fifty six, giving minus four hundred and eighty six kilojoules per mole. questions.modelAnswer:
**Bonds broken.** Two H–H and one O=O: $2 \times 436 + 498 = 1370$ kJ/mol.

**Bonds formed.** Two water molecules, each with **two** O–H bonds, so **four** in total: $4 \times 464 = 1856$ kJ/mol.

**Overall change.** Broken minus formed:

$$1370 - 1856 = \mathbf{-486} \text{ kJ/mol}$$

**Conclusion.** The change is **negative**, so more energy was released forming bonds than was needed to break them. Energy has been transferred to the surroundings, so the reaction is **exothermic** — as burning should be.

The mark most often lost is counting two O–H bonds instead of four.

questions.prompt: Explain how a reaction profile shows whether a reaction is exothermic, and explain why a reaction that releases a great deal of energy may still need to be started with a spark.
questions.solution: A reaction profile plots energy on the vertical axis against the progress of the reaction along the horizontal axis. The reactants are drawn as a level line on the left and the products as a level line on the right. If the products are lower than the reactants then the chemicals have lost energy, which has been transferred to the surroundings, and the reaction is exothermic. The overall energy change is the vertical difference between those two levels. Separately from this, the curved line joining the reactants to the products rises to a peak before coming down, and the height of that peak above the reactants level is the activation energy. The activation energy is the minimum energy that colliding particles must have in order to react. A reaction such as the combustion of petrol has products far below the reactants, so it releases a great deal of energy, but it also has a large activation energy, so the particles do not have enough energy to react at room temperature. A spark supplies that activation energy to a few particles, and once the reaction starts the energy it releases supplies the activation energy for the rest.

questions.modelAnswer:
**Reading the profile.** Energy runs up the vertical axis, progress of the reaction along the horizontal. The **reactants** are a level line on the left, the **products** a level line on the right. **Products below reactants** means the chemicals have **lost** energy to the surroundings, so the reaction is **exothermic**. The **overall change** is the vertical gap between the two levels.

**The hump.** The curve joining them rises to a **peak**. Its height **above the reactants level** is the **activation energy**: the minimum energy colliding particles must have to react.

**Why a spark is needed.** Burning petrol has products far below the reactants, so it releases a great deal of energy — but it also has a **large activation energy**, and at room temperature the particles do not have it. A **spark supplies it** to a few particles; the energy those release then supplies the activation energy for the rest, and the reaction sustains itself.

The two quantities are **independent**: a large release and a large push to start are perfectly compatible.

examTechnique.body:
For a profile, draw the axes first, then the two levels, then the curve, then the arrows. The **activation energy arrow starts at the reactants**, not at the bottom of the axis, and ends at the **peak**. The overall change arrow runs between the two **levels**.

To decide exothermic or endothermic from a profile, look only at where the products sit. Ignore the hump.

For a bond energy calculation, set it out in the same order every time: bonds broken and their total, bonds formed and their total, then broken minus formed. Write each total on its own line so the method marks are visible even if the arithmetic slips.

Count bonds, not molecules. Two waters give four O–H bonds.

Read the sign and say what it means. A bare number with no statement about exothermic or endothermic leaves a mark behind.

If asked why a calculated value differs from a measured one, say that bond energies are mean values, so the calculation is an estimate.
examinerErrors: Measuring the activation energy from the bottom of the axis instead of from the reactants level.
Deciding exothermic or endothermic from the height of the hump rather than the position of the products.
Doing formed minus broken, which reverses the sign and the conclusion.
Counting two O–H bonds for two water molecules instead of four.
Giving a number with no statement of whether the reaction is exothermic or endothermic.
Saying a catalyst changes the overall energy change. It lowers the activation energy only.
Claiming bond energies must be recalled. They are always given.
Treating a calculated change as exact, when bond energies are mean values.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A top answer separates the two quantities without being asked, saying that the activation energy governs how hard the reaction is to start while the position of the products governs whether it is exothermic. It sets a bond energy calculation out in a fixed order, writes each total on its own line, and counts bonds by drawing or listing the molecules rather than trusting the coefficients. It explains the sign rather than remembering it, pointing out that the number describes the chemicals, so a loss of energy from them is negative. It knows bond energies are means and so calls its answer an estimate, and it knows a catalyst moves the hump and nothing else.
